newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada closer to resuming salmon talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada closer to resuming salmon talks.

text.p: The United States and Canada edged closer on Wednesday to resuming talks on fishing rights after a high-level emergency meeting defused tensions spawned by a bitter dispute over the Pacific salmon catch.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy and Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott met a day after Canadian fisherman released an Alaskan ferry they had held captive in Prince Rupert, British Columbia, for three days to protest alleged U.S. overfishing of salmon in the Pacific.
"Both sides are looking at a way to get to negotiations. We are looking at a facilitating mechanism that would be a step toward this," State Department spokesman James Foley told reporters.
Foley said Axworthy had requested the meeting on Tuesday and Talbott, concerned about the urgency of the situation, readily agreed.
"Both nations felt it was imperative to speak directly at a high level ... remember we're talking about the oldest and closest friends in the world," Foley said.

Months of stormy negotiations between Canadian and U.S officials on how to divide this year's Pacific salmon catch broke down last month. U.S. officials have denied breaching any international agreements and said Canada was responsible for the collapse.
The Canadian fishermen contend that Alaskans have taken almost four times as much sockeye salmon this season as allowed under a 1985 Pacific Salmon treaty.
Both Foley and Axworthy described the hour-long meeting as "very good and friendly" and said each side had agreed on the importance of saving the treaty and finding a way to reinvigorate the talks.

Axworthy expressed regret over the U.S. decision to reject Canada's request to send the dispute to arbitration, but "took it on board" and agreed to focus on ways of boosting negotiations and avoiding future incidents such as the Prince Rupert blockade, the spokesman said.

Foley declined to be specific about the "facilitating mechanism" the two sides agreed upon, but said it would bring the two countries "a step closer" to the resumption of talks. An announcement was expected later on Wednesday, he added.
Canadian fishermen have given the Ottawa government one week to make progress on resolving the dispute and threatened further action if it failed to do so.
The three-day blockade of the Alaskan passenger ferry Malaspina escalated the festering salmon squabble and threatened to damage relations between the United States and its biggest trading partner.
Sen. Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, and other lawmakers have urged retaliation, including using U.S. Navy or Coast Guard vessels to protect Alaskan ferries sailing through Canadian waters.

Murkowski, along with Republican Sens. Ted Stevens of Alaska and Slade Gorton of Washington State, introduced a resolution on Wednesday condemning the Canadian government "for failing to accept responsibility" for the blockade and calling on President Bill Clinton to take action.

Among other suggested retaliatory moves were targeting Canadian imports into the United States, banning Americans from bringing British Columbia salmon or shellfish back from sport-fishing trips to Canada, and requiring Canadian ships to seek formal clearance from U.S. Customs before anchoring in U.S. waters off Alaska or other states.
